title: Xinzuo Academy
subtitle: Interactive staff training from The Gongfu of Xinzuo

levels.title: Base
levels.purpose: Recognize the full map of kitchen-knife knowledge and apply safe, correct first principles across every major theme of The Gongfu of Xinzuo.

modules.title: Anatomy & Construction
modules.summary: Name the main parts and understand basic construction terms without turning them into quality slogans.

lessons.title: Blade anatomy and the cutting edge

content.lead: Accurate knife knowledge starts by naming the parts correctly.
points: The spine is the normally unsharpened upper side; the heel is the rear of the cutting edge.
The cutting edge — in this guide, filo and tagliente are synonyms — is the sharpened boundary of the blade.
A bevel is the sloping geometry that leads toward the apex; surface finish is a separate characteristic.
content.takeaway: First identify the feature; then explain what it does.

question.prompt: Which term names the rear part of the cutting edge?

options.text: Heel
Spine
Tip
Bolster

question.explanation: The heel is the rear section of the sharpened edge, close to the handle.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates bevel from finish?

options.text: Bevel and finish are two names for the same feature.
Finish sets the tang type; bevel sets the handle shape.
Bevel describes geometry; finish describes the blade surface.
Finish is the edge angle; bevel is only decoration.

recovery_questions.explanation: Geometry and surface appearance must not be confused.

content.lead: Construction terms describe how the knife is built; they do not create an automatic quality ranking.
points: A full tang follows most of the handle outline; a hidden tang is enclosed inside the handle.
A through tang reaches the butt but is not simply another name for a full tang.
Forging describes a manufacturing step, not a guarantee of superior geometry, heat treatment or finish.
content.takeaway: Judge the complete construction, not one label.

question.prompt: What does a full tang mainly describe?

options.text: How hard the cutting edge has been heat treated
How many layers are visible on the blade face
How symmetrical the edge bevel has been ground
How far the blade steel extends through the handle

question.explanation: Tang terminology describes handle construction, not hardness or bevel geometry.

recovery_questions.prompt: A knife has a welded bolster. What can that fact prove by itself?

options.text: Only how that part was assembled, not overall quality
That the blade steel is automatically low grade
That the knife cannot have good heat treatment
That the edge geometry must be thick and robust

recovery_questions.explanation: A construction detail must be evaluated together with execution and the rest of the knife.

questions.prompt: Where is the cutting edge?

options.text: Along the normally blunt spine
Along the sharpened boundary of the blade
Inside the handle around the tang
Only at the front tip of the knife

questions.explanation: The cutting edge is the sharpened boundary, not the spine or handle.

questions.prompt: Which statement about forging is sound?

options.text: It guarantees a thinner edge than every stamped blade.
It guarantees higher hardness regardless of steel choice.
It is a process step; final quality still depends on many other factors.
It guarantees a full tang and a welded bolster together.

questions.explanation: Forging alone cannot establish the final performance of a knife.

modules.title: Steel Properties
modules.summary: Use a five-dimension framework instead of judging steel by HRC or a single marketing claim.

lessons.title: The five dimensions of knife steel

content.lead: Steel performance is a balance of properties, not a single number.
points: The five teaching dimensions are hardness, sharpening response, corrosion resistance, toughness and microstructural fineness.
HRC measures resistance to permanent deformation; it does not directly measure sharpness or overall quality.
The useful balance depends on the knife, the task and the user.
content.takeaway: Do not rank steels by one property alone.

question.prompt: Which property is measured by HRC?

options.text: Sharpness
Hardness
Toughness
Corrosion resistance

question.explanation: Rockwell C is a hardness scale; the other properties require different evidence.

recovery_questions.prompt: Two steels have the same HRC. What is the safest conclusion?

options.text: They must hold an edge for exactly the same time.
They must contain the same carbide population.
They must resist corrosion to the same degree.
They can still differ in wear, toughness and sharpening response.

recovery_questions.explanation: Hardness is only one part of steel behaviour.

content.lead: Corrosion resistance and sharpening response are both system properties.
points: Stainless classification commonly starts at about 10.5% chromium by mass, but corrosion resistance still varies widely.
Chromium supports passivation; salt, acids and prolonged wetness can still stain or pit stainless steel.
The shortcut 'softer steel is easier to sharpen' is unreliable because matrix and carbides also control abrasion and burr behaviour.
content.takeaway: Stainless is corrosion-resistant, not stain-proof.

question.prompt: Which statement about stainless knife steel is correct?

options.text: It cannot stain if chromium exceeds the stainless threshold.
It never needs attention after acidic or salty foods.
It resists corrosion but still benefits from prompt cleaning and drying.
Its corrosion resistance is determined by HRC alone.

question.explanation: Stainless steels vary, and normal care still matters.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can a harder carbon steel sometimes sharpen cleanly on water stones?

options.text: Hardness automatically makes every abrasive cut faster.
Sharpening response also depends on microstructure, carbides and burr behaviour.
Carbon steel contains no hard particles at all.
Water stones ignore hardness once they are wet.

recovery_questions.explanation: Hardness alone does not predict sharpening feel.

questions.prompt: What is the best first question when comparing steels?

options.text: Which balance of properties suits this use?
Which steel has the highest HRC number?
Which steel has the longest alloying list?
Which steel has the most expensive name?

questions.explanation: Steel selection begins from use and trade-offs, not a single prestige signal.

questions.prompt: What does passivation mainly do?

options.text: Turns the entire blade into a harder martensitic phase
Removes every carbide from the steel matrix
Makes the edge angle smaller during normal use
Forms a thin protective oxide layer at the surface

questions.explanation: Passivation slows corrosion at the surface; it is not a hardening process.

modules.title: Metallurgy & Heat Treatment
modules.summary: Understand the basic chain from composition to microstructure, heat treatment and powder metallurgy.

content.lead: Chemical composition matters, but it is the starting point rather than the complete performance specification.
points: Carbon enables high hardness; chromium supports stainless behaviour; molybdenum can aid hardenability and pitting resistance.
Vanadium, tungsten and niobium can form very hard carbides that raise wear resistance but may slow sharpening.
More alloying is not automatically better because elements interact with heat treatment and microstructure.
content.takeaway: Composition defines potential; processing turns it into performance.

question.prompt: What is the safest use of an alloy composition table?

options.text: Use it as one input together with heat treatment and geometry.
Use it to rank every knife without looking at construction.
Use the number of elements as a direct quality score.
Use chromium percentage as a complete cutting-performance rating.

question.explanation: Composition alone does not determine the finished knife.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which element is most directly associated with stainless passivation?

options.text: Tungsten
Cobalt
Chromium
Vanadium

recovery_questions.explanation: Chromium is the central alloying element behind stainless passivation.

lessons.title: Heat treatment, carbides and powder metallurgy

content.lead: Steel chemistry must be converted into a useful microstructure by processing and heat treatment.
points: Austenitizing prepares the high-temperature phase; quenching forms hard martensitic structure; tempering makes that structure usable.
Retained austenite can be reduced by suitable sub-zero or deep-freeze processing in demanding steels.
Powder metallurgy can improve uniformity and carbide distribution compared with conventional solidification, especially in highly alloyed steels.
content.takeaway: Steelmaking route and heat treatment shape the microstructure you actually cut with.

question.prompt: What is the main purpose of tempering after hardening?

options.text: Add chromium to the steel after the blade is finished
Create the handle material around the finished tang
Turn a double bevel into a single bevel by heating
Make the hardened structure usable by adjusting its properties

question.explanation: Tempering follows hardening to balance the final martensitic structure.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why is powder metallurgy useful in high-alloy steels?

options.text: It can produce a finer, more uniform distribution of alloy-rich particles.
It removes the need for any later heat treatment.
It guarantees that every powder steel is tougher than every conventional steel.
It makes carbide type irrelevant to sharpening behaviour.

recovery_questions.explanation: Powder metallurgy changes solidification and distribution; it does not eliminate trade-offs.

questions.prompt: What can very hard carbides generally increase?

options.text: Handle moisture resistance
Abrasive wear resistance
Blade length during sharpening
Tang size inside the handle

questions.explanation: Hard carbides can improve wear resistance, with sharpening trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Which phase is the hard structure sought by quenching knife steel?

options.text: Austenite
Ferrite
Martensite
Graphite

questions.explanation: Quenching is used to form martensitic structure from the high-temperature condition.

modules.title: Xinzuo Steels & Handle Materials
modules.summary: Recognize the main material families and explain them as design choices rather than rankings.

lessons.title: Read the Xinzuo steel range by design goal

content.lead: The Xinzuo range uses different steels because different knives and users need different balances.
points: Premium powder steels such as ZDP-189, SRS13 and M390 pursue different combinations of hardness, wear resistance and corrosion behaviour.
10Cr15CoMoV, 12Cr18MoV, AUS-10, VG10 and 14C28N occupy different all-round stainless positions rather than one simple ranking.
Blue Steel No. 2 trades stainless convenience for responsive carbon-steel behaviour; 1.4116 occupies a more forgiving moderate-hardness position.
content.takeaway: Choose the balance, not the most prestigious steel name.

question.prompt: Which statement best describes the Xinzuo steel range?

options.text: Every newer steel is automatically better for every customer.
Different steels target different balances of properties and use.
HRC alone determines which steel belongs at the top.
Carbon steels are always easier choices than stainless steels.

question.explanation: The range is deliberately diverse because needs differ.

recovery_questions.prompt: What is the basic trade-off of Blue Steel No. 2 in this range?

options.text: Complete rust immunity in exchange for very low hardness
No sharpening response in exchange for maximum chromium
Very soft matrix in exchange for a ceramic-like handle
Reactive carbon-steel care in exchange for responsive sharpening behaviour

recovery_questions.explanation: Blue Steel No. 2 is valued for carbon-steel behaviour, with corresponding care needs.

lessons.title: Handle materials change feel and care

content.lead: A handle material should be judged by how it changes the complete knife, not by prestige alone.
points: Technical materials such as PP, ABS, G10 and carbon-fibre composites emphasize different balances of moisture resistance, weight and feel.
Micarta, pakka wood and stabilized wood combine fibres or wood with resins to change stability and maintenance.
Natural woods vary in density, grain and care needs; material name alone does not establish ergonomics or quality.
content.takeaway: Material, shape, surface, weight and care must be evaluated together.

question.prompt: What should staff avoid when describing a handle material?

options.text: Explaining how moisture resistance can affect daily use
Comparing weight and surface feel between suitable handles
Treating the material name alone as a complete quality score
Discussing different care needs for natural and technical materials

question.explanation: Handle quality depends on design, execution and fit as well as material.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can a denser handle material change knife feel?

options.text: It automatically changes the chemical composition of the blade.
It can move mass rearward and alter perceived balance.
It forces the cutting edge into a single-bevel geometry.
It removes the need to compare handle shape and circumference.

recovery_questions.explanation: Handle material contributes to mass distribution but does not replace ergonomic evaluation.

mini_test.title: Quick check · Xinzuo Steels & Handle Materials

questions.prompt: When should staff compare exact steel grades?

options.text: After identifying knives whose function already suits the customer
Before asking what the customer cuts or how they work
Instead of checking blade geometry or intended use
Only after choosing the most decorative blade pattern

questions.explanation: Steel is a differentiator among suitable knives, not a substitute for suitability.

questions.prompt: Which handle choice is most defensible?

options.text: The rarest material regardless of grip or working environment
The heaviest handle regardless of the blade's balance
The hardest surface regardless of comfort during repeated use
The one whose material, shape and care fit the user's needs

questions.explanation: The complete hand interface matters more than a material label.

modules.title: Damascus & Layered Construction
modules.summary: Distinguish real layered construction from decoration and understand differential wear without marketing shortcuts.

content.lead: A visible Damascus-like pattern does not, by itself, tell you how the blade was built.
points: Pattern-welded Damascus is created from real layers joined and manipulated through the blade construction.
Laser or other surface decoration can imitate a pattern without creating a layered structure.
Layer count can describe construction complexity, but it is not a direct sharpness or quality score.
content.takeaway: First identify the construction; only then discuss the pattern.

question.prompt: What best distinguishes genuine layered Damascus from a laser pattern?

options.text: The pattern comes from joined material layers rather than surface marking.
The genuine blade always has the highest HRC in the range.
The genuine blade always contains more chromium than any monosteel.
The laser pattern can be identified only by the handle material.

question.explanation: Construction, not visual complexity alone, defines layered Damascus.

recovery_questions.prompt: What does a higher layer count prove on its own?

options.text: A sharper apex regardless of sharpening and edge geometry
Greater toughness regardless of steel and heat treatment
More layers in the stated construction, not automatically better cutting
Higher corrosion resistance regardless of alloy composition

recovery_questions.explanation: Layer count is descriptive; performance still follows the complete design.

content.lead: Full-Damascus blades can develop a changing microscopic edge texture as different layers wear at different rates.
points: Differential wear can preserve slicing bite even as peak sharpness gradually declines.
This is not literal automatic sharpening and it does not remove the need for maintenance.
Sharpness and slicing bite are related but not identical sensations.
content.takeaway: Differential wear changes edge character; it does not create a maintenance-free knife.

question.prompt: What can differential wear in full Damascus help preserve?

options.text: A perfectly polished apex without any future sharpening
The exact factory angle regardless of how the knife is used
Complete immunity to chipping under lateral loads
Slicing bite as the microscopic edge texture evolves

question.explanation: The effect concerns edge texture and slicing behaviour, not automatic restoration of factory geometry.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why is 'self-sharpening' potentially misleading for full Damascus?

options.text: The edge still wears and eventually needs normal maintenance.
The blade cannot develop any microscopic texture during use.
The layers all wear at exactly the same rate by definition.
The effect exists only on laser-decorated monosteel blades.

recovery_questions.explanation: Differential wear may change bite, but it is not perpetual sharpening.

questions.prompt: Which term should Italian staff reserve for a monosteel blade with a laser-applied Damascus-like pattern?

options.text: Acciaio Damasco stratificato
Damascato superficialmente
Damasco integrale saldato
Pacchetto Damasco strutturale

questions.explanation: In this guide 'damascato' is reserved for surface decoration, not genuine layered Damascus.

questions.prompt: Which two ideas should be kept separate?

options.text: Blade length and handle colour
Tang shape and packaging size
Peak sharpness and slicing bite
Logo position and Rockwell scale

questions.explanation: A toothier edge can keep useful slicing bite even when peak refinement changes.

modules.title: Geometry & Bevels
modules.summary: Recognize the main bevel families and the basic consequences of symmetry, asymmetry and single-bevel construction.

content.lead: Bevel names describe how steel supports and guides the edge; they are not quality rankings.
points: Common families include symmetrical V, convex, asymmetric V, compound V, hollow, single-sided and single-sided with urasuki.
A compound edge separates the broad primary geometry from the small edge bevel used in routine sharpening.
Strength and cutting resistance depend on thickness, angle, steel and support, not simply on bevel count.
content.takeaway: Read the cross-section before making claims about behaviour.

question.prompt: Which part is normally restored in routine sharpening of a compound double-V edge?

options.text: The entire broad primary grind every time
The small edge bevel at the apex
The spine thickness along the full blade
The tang surface inside the handle scales

question.explanation: Routine sharpening restores the edge bevel; thinning the primary geometry is a different operation.

recovery_questions.prompt: Does a double bevel always mean a perfect 50/50 geometry?

options.text: Yes; any asymmetry would make it a single bevel.
Yes; only handle geometry can be asymmetric.
No; because double bevel means the spine is sharpened too.
No; both sides are sharpened, but the proportions can differ.

recovery_questions.explanation: Bevel count and exact symmetry are separate properties.

content.lead: Strong asymmetry can create handedness and directional behaviour that must be checked model by model.
points: A traditional single-bevel knife places the main bevel on one side; many specialist forms use an urasuki hollow on the reverse.
The urasuki is a functional hollow with narrow reference lands, not an unfinished back surface.
Sharpening must preserve the existing geometry; do not turn the reverse into a normal double-bevel facet.
content.takeaway: Check the exact grind and lateral orientation before advising use or sharpening.

question.prompt: What is the urasuki on a traditional single-bevel knife?

options.text: A decorative laser pattern on the main bevel
A second normal edge bevel at the same angle
A shallow functional hollow on the reverse face
A full tang visible along the handle outline

question.explanation: The urasuki is part of the specialist working geometry.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can a strongly asymmetric edge steer?

options.text: The handle colour changes friction at the cutting edge.
The two sides displace food differently as the blade advances.
The HRC number pulls the blade toward the harder side.
The tang becomes magnetized by repeated sharpening.

recovery_questions.explanation: Directional behaviour comes from asymmetric working geometry.

questions.prompt: What can a convex section generally change compared with a similar flat section?

options.text: How material supports the edge and separates food
Whether the steel becomes stainless during use
Whether the tang reaches the end of the handle
Whether the knife was packed in a wooden box

questions.explanation: Cross-section geometry influences support and cutting interaction.

questions.prompt: Before giving handedness advice, what should staff verify?

options.text: Only the silhouette and country of origin
Only the handle material and blade length
Only whether the blade has a Damascus pattern
The exact model's grind and orientation

questions.explanation: A traditional profile name alone does not prove the exact grind.

modules.title: Knife Families & Ergonomics
modules.summary: Match blade families to tasks and understand how weight, balance and grip affect the choice.

content.lead: Knife names are useful only when they connect to the mechanical work a blade is designed to do.
points: Chef's knife, gyuto, santoku, bunka and many Chinese cleavers can be multi-use tools with different profiles and movement preferences.
Boning, filleting, fish butchery and long slicing need specialist geometries rather than simply more force.
Bread, frozen food and other hard-food tasks can require serrated or dedicated tools.
content.takeaway: Start from the work; then choose the knife family.

question.prompt: What should staff identify before recommending a blade family?

options.text: The foods, quantities and cutting movements involved
The most decorative pattern currently in stock
The highest hardness number on the product list
The most expensive handle material in the display

question.explanation: Functional requirements come before appearance or prestige.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which statement about a thin Chinese cleaver is safest?

options.text: Every Chinese cleaver is intended for heavy bone impact.
Every Chinese cleaver must use single-bevel geometry.
It can be a board-oriented multi-use knife and not a bone chopper.
Every Chinese cleaver is unsuitable for vegetable work.

recovery_questions.explanation: The family name does not override the exact geometry and intended use.

lessons.title: Weight, balance and grip change handling

content.lead: Two knives with similar steel and geometry can feel very different because mass distribution and grip change leverage.
points: More mass can add momentum but also needs more effort to start, stop and redirect.
Blade-forward, neutral and rearward balance feel different even at the same total weight.
Moving from a handle grip toward a pinch grip changes perceived balance because the hand moves closer to blade mass.
content.takeaway: Evaluate balance in the user's real grip, not from a specification sheet alone.

question.prompt: Why can the same knife feel better balanced in a pinch grip?

options.text: The blade physically becomes lighter when touched forward.
The steel hardness falls when the hand crosses the bolster.
The tang shortens as the hand moves toward the blade.
The controlling fingers move closer to the blade's mass.

question.explanation: Grip position changes leverage, not the knife's actual mass.

recovery_questions.prompt: Two suitable knives weigh the same but feel different. What should staff compare?

options.text: Mass distribution, handle shape and the customer's grip
Only the printed total weight on the product card
Only the country in which the steel was developed
Only the number of decorative layers in the blade

recovery_questions.explanation: Ergonomic fit depends on where mass and the hand meet.

questions.prompt: Why is a long slicer long?

options.text: To increase sideways leverage around hard joints
To use more edge in a smooth drawing cut
To make the knife suitable for striking frozen food
To move the balance as far behind the handle as possible

questions.explanation: Length helps when the cutting movement actually uses that edge length.

questions.prompt: What is the correct recommendation sequence?

options.text: Appearance → hardness → function
Price → pattern → handle length
Function → ergonomics → selection
Steel grade → box → cutting task

questions.explanation: Solve the work first, then fit, then select among suitable products.

modules.title: Cutting Techniques
modules.summary: Recognize the main movement paths and use specialist techniques without forcing the blade.

content.lead: Technique begins by observing the path of the edge rather than memorizing labels.
points: Direct descent suits fairly flat edge sections; an advancing stroke combines forward and downward travel.
Long slicing uses a draw through the food, spreading work across more edge length.
Rocking keeps a changing contact point and works best with suitable belly curvature.
content.takeaway: Choose a movement that matches edge shape and food instead of forcing the knife.

question.prompt: Which movement adds forward travel while the blade descends?

options.text: Pure direct descent
Advancing push cut
Static in-hand peeling
Sideways board scraping

question.explanation: The advancing stroke combines slicing travel with descent.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why does a long drawing stroke help a slicer?

options.text: It increases sideways pressure so the blade can lever food apart.
It keeps one point of the tip fixed on the board at all times.
It makes edge geometry irrelevant once enough speed is reached.
It spreads the cut over more edge and reduces repeated sawing.

recovery_questions.explanation: Long slicing works because the stroke actually uses the available edge length.

lessons.title: Use specialist movements within their limits

content.lead: Fine work, bone work, filleting and in-hand tasks require control rather than extra force.
points: The supporting hand should be set before the blade moves, with fingertips protected from the cutting path.
Work around bones and joints follows anatomy; do not use a fine blade as a lever.
Filleting follows contours with only the flex designed into the knife; specialist techniques that need demonstration should not be improvised.
content.takeaway: Control the path first; force is never a substitute for fit.

question.prompt: When should the supporting hand be positioned?

options.text: After the first cut reveals the blade path
Only when cutting very small ingredients
Before the knife starts moving
Only when using a forward pinch grip

question.explanation: Hand position establishes the safe path before movement.

recovery_questions.prompt: A hard fillet knife reaches its natural flex limit. What should the user do?

options.text: Twist the handle until the blade follows the contour.
Change the cutting angle rather than forcing more bend.
Lever against the bones to increase the available bend.
Strike the spine so the blade flexes through the section.

recovery_questions.explanation: Use only the flex the model is designed to provide.

questions.prompt: A very flat edge leaves uncut skins during pure rocking. What is the likely issue?

options.text: The movement does not match the blade curvature well.
The handle material is absorbing too much moisture.
The steel contains too little chromium for the board.
The tang is too long for a repeated cutting motion.

questions.explanation: Technique should follow the geometry of the edge.

questions.prompt: What is the safest principle when working around a joint?

options.text: Increase force until the blade crosses the hard point.
Use lateral twist to separate every resistant section.
Hold the food in the air to improve access to the joint.
Follow the anatomy with controlled cuts instead of prying.

questions.explanation: A knife cuts; it should not be used as a pry bar.

modules.title: Safe Use & Handling
modules.summary: Make safety a complete system from workstation setup through washing, carrying and storage.

content.lead: Most safe knife handling is decided before the blade starts moving.
points: Stable board, stable food, clear cutting path and protected fingertips form the basic pre-cut check.
Use the right knife for the task and only the force the cut requires.
Avoid twisting, sideways levering and scraping the board with the cutting edge.
content.takeaway: If the setup is unstable, the cut is not ready.

question.prompt: A round ingredient rolls on the board. What comes first?

options.text: Create a stable flat support before the main cut.
Grip it harder with exposed fingertips near the blade.
Use a faster stroke so the food has less time to move.
Choose a heavier knife and increase downward pressure.

question.explanation: Mechanical stability should be corrected before adding movement or force.

recovery_questions.prompt: A thin hard blade binds in dense food. What is the safe response?

options.text: Twist the handle gently until the food opens.
Use the blade face as a lever to widen the gap.
Withdraw it carefully and change the cut.
Strike the spine while keeping the blade trapped.

recovery_questions.explanation: Twisting creates damaging lateral load; change the cut instead.

content.lead: Washing, passing, carrying and storage are still knife-handling tasks.
points: Never hide a sharp knife under soapy water or among objects in a sink.
Pass the handle deliberately; for short movement carry the knife low, still and with a predictable path.
If a knife falls, do not try to catch it; step away and let it fall.
content.takeaway: A knife must remain visible, controlled and predictable even when it is not cutting.

question.prompt: A knife slips from the counter. What should you do?

options.text: Catch the handle before the blade reaches the floor.
Block the blade with a foot to protect the edge.
Reach with both hands so one can stop the knife.
Move away and let it fall.

question.explanation: Trying to catch a falling knife creates an unnecessary injury risk.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which washing habit is unsafe?

options.text: Leaving the knife hidden in a sink of soapy water
Washing one knife at a time with the edge visible
Keeping the handle controlled while cleaning the blade
Drying the blade and handle promptly after rinsing

recovery_questions.explanation: Hidden blades can injure someone who reaches into the sink.

questions.prompt: Which is part of the four-point safety check?

options.text: Maximum downward force
Clear blade path
Wet cutting board surface
Exposed guiding fingertips

questions.explanation: A clear path is one of the basic pre-cut conditions.

questions.prompt: How should a knife be passed to another person?

options.text: Quickly, with the blade presented so it stays visible
Wrapped loosely in a towel with no clear orientation
Deliberately, with the handle presented and edge controlled
Balanced flat on the open palm while both people move

questions.explanation: Predictable orientation and control reduce transfer risk.

modules.title: Care & Cutting Boards
modules.summary: Protect the edge and materials through suitable boards, cleaning, drying, storage and appropriate maintenance.

lessons.title: Choose cutting boards by edge interaction

content.lead: The cutting board is part of the edge system because every board cut ends in surface contact.
points: Suitable wood, purpose-made plastic and resilient synthetic boards can be edge-friendly when clean, flat and stable.
End-grain wood lets fibres separate and recover more readily under the edge than many harder surfaces.
Glass, stone, ceramic and metal are too unyielding for routine work with fine kitchen edges.
content.takeaway: Judge a board by what it does to the edge as well as hygiene and care.

question.prompt: Which surface should be avoided for routine cutting with a fine edge?

options.text: Suitable wood
Glass
Purpose-made plastic
Resilient synthetic board

question.explanation: Glass is hard and unyielding at the moment of edge contact.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can end-grain wood be gentle on an edge?

options.text: It is harder than glass and therefore stops the edge sooner.
It chemically hardens the apex during every board contact.
It prevents all moisture from entering any type of wood.
Its fibre orientation can let fibres separate under the edge.

recovery_questions.explanation: Fibre orientation is one reason end grain can be edge-friendly.

content.lead: Good maintenance removes avoidable moisture, corrosion, impact and edge-contact risks.
points: Wash by hand, rinse salt and acids promptly, and dry blade and handle completely.
Carbon steel may develop a stable dark patina; active orange rust is different and should be addressed.
A honing rod can realign or maintain some edges, but it does not replace sharpening when the apex needs material removal.
content.takeaway: Prevent damage early instead of repairing it later.

question.prompt: What should happen after cutting salty or acidic food?

options.text: Leave the residue until the next normal washing cycle.
Soak the blade overnight to dissolve the remaining residue.
Rinse promptly and dry the knife completely.
Store the knife wet so the passive layer can form faster.

question.explanation: Removing salts, acids and moisture reduces unnecessary corrosion risk.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which statement about patina on carbon steel is correct?

options.text: Any colour change means the blade has structurally failed.
A stable dark patina is different from active orange rust.
Orange rust is a protective patina that should be preserved.
Patina proves the steel has become stainless during use.

recovery_questions.explanation: Patina and active rust are chemically and practically different conditions.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to compare board materials?

options.text: Compare edge friendliness, stability, hygiene and maintenance.
Choose the hardest surface because it lasts longest.
Choose only by whether the board can enter a dishwasher.
Choose only by appearance and ignore surface hardness.

questions.explanation: Board materials involve several practical trade-offs.

questions.prompt: When is a honing rod not a substitute for sharpening?

options.text: Whenever the handle is made from a technical composite
Whenever the knife is stored in a fitted blade guard
Whenever the cutting board is made from end-grain wood
When the apex needs abrasive material removal to be restored

questions.explanation: Honing and sharpening are different maintenance operations.

modules.title: Sharpening & Edge Maintenance
modules.summary: Build a repeatable basic process from stone setup and bevel contact through burr control and testing.

lessons.title: Set up the stone and verify contact

content.lead: Good sharpening begins with a stable, suitable stone and visible control of the edge bevel.
points: Follow the stone maker's water or lubrication instructions; not every water stone should be soaked.
The working surface should be flat enough and the support should not move.
Marker on the edge bevel shows where the abrasive is actually contacting and helps correct the angle.
content.takeaway: Stable stone, correct contact, complete edge coverage.

question.prompt: The stone holder moves during a sharpening pass. What should you do?

options.text: Stop and stabilize it before continuing.
Increase pressure so the blade holds the stone in place.
Move faster so the support has less time to shift.
Change to a finer grit without correcting the support.

question.explanation: A moving stone compromises both safety and angle control.

recovery_questions.prompt: What does the marker method verify?

options.text: The exact HRC value of the steel after tempering
The carbide chemistry of the alloy under the microscope
Where the stone contacts and removes material on the edge bevel
The tang construction hidden inside the knife handle

recovery_questions.explanation: Ink removal makes sharpening contact visible.

lessons.title: Use the burr as evidence, then remove it

content.lead: The burr proves that abrasion reached the apex; it is not the desired final edge.
points: Aim for the smallest detectable burr that is continuous from heel to tip.
Reduce pressure and alternate sides during deburring until no directional hook remains.
Final testing should combine visual or burr checks with controlled cuts; paper alone can be fooled by a fragile wire edge.
content.takeaway: A good edge is clean, stable and consistent along its full length.

question.prompt: What does a burr present only in the middle prove?

options.text: The entire edge is finished from heel to tip.
The sharpening angle is perfect along the full blade.
The stone is too fine for any further work.
Only the middle has reached the apex.

question.explanation: A continuous burr is needed as evidence of complete apex reach on that side.

recovery_questions.prompt: What should happen to pressure during deburring?

options.text: Reduce it progressively while alternating sides.
Increase it steadily until the burr becomes larger.
Remain at maximum pressure on one side only.
Stop contacting the edge bevel before the burr is removed.

recovery_questions.explanation: Light alternating passes weaken and remove the burr while stabilizing the apex.

questions.prompt: Why must hand position adapt near a curved tip?

options.text: To create the largest possible burr only at the tip
To preserve local bevel contact as the blade profile changes
To polish the blade face instead of working the edge
To keep the wrist fixed while the contact point moves away

questions.explanation: The hand follows the changing geometry to keep the intended contact.

questions.prompt: Why should paper not be the only final sharpness test?

options.text: Paper can never reveal a catch or rough section in an edge.
Paper always damages every properly sharpened kitchen knife.
A fragile wire edge can cut paper yet fail in food.
Paper works only on serrated knives and not on plain edges.

questions.explanation: Use multiple checks to distinguish a stable apex from a temporary wire edge.
